problem: VLN agents are evaluated only with episode-level metrics (SR, SPL, nDTW), which say nothing about fine-grained skills such as stopping, turning, or grounding objects and rooms. Prior masking studies also suffer from compounding errors along the trajectory.
motivation: Knowing which sub-instructions agents actually ground is needed to understand what current models can be trusted to do and what needs further work. Controlled interventions where the correct next action is known allow skill-level diagnosis independent of trajectory-level error accumulation.
key_idea: Truncate RxR trajectory-instruction pairs, append a template skill-specific sub-instruction, teacher-force the agent to the truncation point, and measure how its next-action distribution shifts with versus without the intervention.
insight: HAMT grounds unconditional skills (stop, directional turns) strongly but object and room grounding is weak, with errors resembling a forward-bias baseline (the Forward Bias agent gives a similarly shaped angular error distribution), so training biases persist. Across three agents, skill scores rise with RxR performance but not uniformly: HAMT gains mainly on Turn (43.74 vs 27.14 for EnvDrop) while Object stays around 11-13. This suggests VLN progress is driven more by some skills than others.
method: Truncated episodes: use RxR pose-trace alignments to cut each trajectory at node n_j (T-2 candidates per trajectory) with the instruction prefix, from English val-unseen-guide.

Intervention templates: append manually designed templates from common RxR phrases (stop: 'This is your destination.'; direction: 'Turn left and walk forward.'; object/room: 'Walk towards the [X]') using REVERIE objects and Matterport3D room labels.

Per-skill filtering: keep only episodes with both relevant and irrelevant action options (e.g. at least 1 neighbor in the target direction region and at least 2 outside; object within 3m and a neighbor within 15 degrees; a neighbor in a different room type).
Teacher-forced sensitivity measurement: force the agent along tau, record P(a|tau,I) versus P(a|tau,I+I_int) at the last node, and compare distributions rather than argmax actions.
Statistics: hierarchical bootstrap (scene->trajectory) for CIs and linear mixed-effect models (lmer) with random scan/trajectory slopes and intercepts for intervention effects.
Skill score: average probability mass placed on correct actions, Score(f,s)=mean_e sum_{a in N_e} P_f(a|tau_e, I_e+I_int), to compare agents (EnvDrop, EnvDrop ViL-CLIP, HAMT).
k-hop room seeking: run argmax rollouts after the forced prefix and measure the geodesic distance to the nearest node of the target room type.

setting.backbone: HAMT, EnvDrop (ImageNet features), EnvDrop (ViL-CLIP) - pretrained, frozen, analysis only
setting.training_data: Authors' released pretrained checkpoints trained on RxR (no new training)
setting.observation: Panoramic RGB views at Matterport3D navigation-graph nodes
setting.action_space: Discrete nav-graph neighbor viewpoints plus stop
setting.privileged: Analysis uses GT trajectories with teacher forcing, RxR pose-trace alignment, REVERIE object annotations and Matterport3D room labels to build interventions and correct actions

numbers_note: Not a standard-benchmark paper. Skill scores are the only tabulated results; the rest are figures and LMM effect sizes in text. The appendix also has an RxR teacher-forcing check for HAMT (SR 42.49 vs 52.94 with forcing).
results: HAMT stops with probability 0.72 (explicit) versus 0.65 (implicit) and responds strongly to directional language (effects 0.16-0.48), but shows only weak object (0.069) and room (0.26) effects. Skill scores rise from EnvDrop (avg 31.12) to HAMT (avg 38.50), with the largest gain on Turn and none on Object.
limitations: Interventions are simple templates ('Walk towards X') on partial, truncated trajectories, and the intervention episodes are shorter than typical RxR.
Only three agents are analyzed (mainly HAMT), the skill set is small (stop, turn, object, room), and the analysis measures behavior, not why it occurs; causes in the appendix are speculation.
Scores depend on filtering choices and teacher forcing, and object/room grounding is evaluated only on nearby, visible targets.
